rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is and refuses to build stories on borrowed assumptions. Its strongest move is “What Substack's $400M creator number says about Substack's own revenue,” paired with the explicit warning that dividing top-creator earnings by all paid subscriptions is indefensible. B has real angles, but “YouTube runs on ads. Substack's video play bets that creators would rather own their audience” drags in YouTube/TikTok economics and an “own their audience” frame not supplied by the update, then treats inference like fact.
gaps_in_A: The category angle says “video is the piece that makes the category shift hard to argue with”; sharp, but it still needs one adoption proof point before becoming a full category-change story.
“The competitor take rates a reporter will compare against must be supplied” is the right caution, but the set does not prioritize which competitive set to research first.
“Draft the category angle first” is defensible, but the funding-math angle may be just as strong if Substack can clarify whether $400M is gross or net.
gaps_in_B: “YouTube and TikTok monetize through algorithmic distribution and advertising” is outside the supplied update. True enough in the world, but this exercise asked for grounded angles, not memory garnish.
“implying $40M or more flowed to Substack from top creators alone” is too confident. If the $400M figure is net, gross, mixed, or includes non-subscription revenue, the math changes.
“subscription fatigue narrative” depends on an external discourse that was not provided. It can be a story, but here it is a borrowed peg with no supplied evidence.
“a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers” invents a sample creator profile. It is illustrative, but founder-ready angle work cannot smuggle in fake specificity.
